text: The layout is sketched. Now we write the DAX measures that will actually power those KPI cards and that bar chart — and we'll explain each one from scratch, no DAX experience assumed.

First measure, Total Sales, equals sum of RegionalSalesSnapshot TotalSalesAmount. Sum adds up every value currently visible to the measure — all rows if nothing's filtering the report, or just one territory's rows once a slicer narrows it down. Straightforward, and it'll stay correct once filtering gets added next lesson.

Second measure, Order Count, equals sum of OrderCount — and notice that's sum, not count, and not distinct count. That's because the counting already happened back in the T-SQL query. OrderCount is a column of numbers, one already-counted total per territory and product line row. Summing those pre-counted numbers gives the right grand total. Using distinct count here would count how many different OrderCount values show up — a meaningless number, not how many orders there actually were.

Third measure, Average Order Value, equals divide of Total Sales by Order Count. This one references the other two measures by name, not the raw columns, so it automatically inherits their correct behavior under any filter. And it uses divide, not a plain slash, because divide returns blank instead of an error if order count is ever zero for some filtered combination — a real possibility once a region slicer exists.

The lesson underneath all three measures: match the DAX function to what the column actually contains, not to what its name suggests. OrderCount sounds like it wants a counting function, but it already is a count — summing it is what's correct.
Three measures, ready to power the whole report. Next lesson, we add a region slicer and format everything so it reads clearly to a non-technical stakeholder.
